qs.q: A 45-year-old woman with a functioning adrenal tumour undergoes successful surgical resection. In the immediate post-operative recovery period, what metabolic complication must clinicians monitor for alongside hypotension?
o: Severe rebound hyperinsulinaemia leading to hypoglycaemia
Profound hyperkalaemia secondary to mineralocorticoid excess
Acute hypocalcaemia resulting from parathyroid gland suppression
Uncontrolled diabetic ketoacidosis from acute insulin deficiency
qs.e: Post-operative monitoring after phaeochromocytoma resection must include vigilance for hypoglycaemia resulting from rebound hyperinsulinaemia after the inhibitory effect of catecholamines is removed. Hyperkalaemia is not a standard rebound feature of catecholamine withdrawal.

exam: A 45‑year‑old woman with resistant hypertension and hypokalaemia – what is the next diagnostic step and why? — Measure serum aldosterone‑renin ratio; a high ratio points to primary aldosteronism, guiding further confirmatory testing.

During pre‑operative preparation for a suspected pheochromocytoma, which drug class must be started first and what is the risk of omitting it? — Initiate α‑blockade; omission can precipitate intra‑operative hypertensive crisis.

An incidental 3 cm adrenal mass is found on ultrasound in a patient with known breast cancer – how do you decide whether to biopsy? — Avoid FNA unless metastasis is strongly suspected; imaging characteristics and hormone profile are preferred, because biopsy can trigger catecholamine release.

A patient presents with Cushingoid features and a 5 cm adrenal mass on CT – what staging system applies and what does stage II indicate? — ENSAT staging; stage II means tumour >5 cm but confined to the gland, indicating surgical removal is curative in most cases.

What are the key intra‑operative precautions for a pheochromocytoma resection in a low‑resource setting? — Ensure adequate α‑blockade, have rapid‑acting IV antihypertensives (e.g., nitroprusside) ready, monitor invasive BP, and avoid tumor manipulation until blockade is effective.

How would you manage postoperative adrenal insufficiency after bilateral adrenalectomy in a patient with limited access to hydrocortisone? — Provide oral prednisolone (available in most formularies) and educate on stress‑dose rules; arrange regular follow‑up for dose titration.
Why is a lipid‑rich adenoma typically benign on MRI chemical shift imaging? — Lipid causes signal loss on out‑of‑phase images, a hallmark of benign adenomas, helping avoid unnecessary surgery.

In a patient with HIV and a 7 cm adrenal mass, what additional investigations are warranted before surgery? — Screen for opportunistic infections (TB, fungal) with chest X‑ray and sputum, and assess CD4 count to optimise peri‑operative care.
ai.title: Adrenal Tumours
ai.subject: Surgery
ai.summary: Adrenal tumours range from benign adenomas to malignant carcinomas and hormone‑producing lesions. Diagnosis relies on imaging, hormonal tests and size criteria, while management balances surgical removal with medical control of excess hormones.

b: Benign adenoma: <4 cm, homogeneous, low attenuation on CT, no hormone excess.
Malignant carcinoma: >6 cm, irregular borders, necrosis, possible metastases.
Functional tumour: excess hormone production (cortisol, aldosterone, catecholamines).
sections.p: An adrenal tumour is any abnormal growth arising from the cortex or medulla of the adrenal gland, identified on imaging or incidentally during surgery.

b: Stage I: ≤5 cm, confined to gland.
Stage II: >5 cm, confined to gland.
Stage III: Local invasion or nodal disease.
Stage IV: Distant metastasis.
sections.p: Malignant adrenal cortical carcinoma is staged by the ENSAT system (size, local invasion, nodal involvement, distant metastasis). Benign lesions are staged by size and functional status.

b: Non‑functioning cortical adenoma – most frequent incidentaloma.
Cortisol‑producing adenoma – Cushing’s syndrome.
Aldosterone‑producing adenoma – primary aldosteronism.
Pheochromocytoma – catecholamine excess.
Adrenocortical carcinoma – rare, aggressive.
Metastases from lung, breast, melanoma – consider in cancer patients.
sections.p: Most adrenal masses are non‑functioning adenomas; functional tumours are less common but clinically important.

b: Incidental finding on abdominal ultrasound/CT.
Cushing’s syndrome: central obesity, hypertension, glucose intolerance.
Primary aldosteronism: resistant hypertension, hypokalaemia, muscle cramps.
Pheochromocytoma: episodic headache, palpitations, sweating, hypertension.
Carcinoma: abdominal pain, weight loss, palpable mass, early satiety.
sections.p: Presentation depends on size, invasiveness and hormone secretion.
Combine imaging with targeted hormonal assays; adapt when tests are unavailable.

t.b: Is the lesion benign‑appearing or suspicious? → Size > 6 cm, irregular borders, high attenuation suggest malignancy.
Does the mass lose signal on out‑of‑phase images? → Signal loss indicates lipid‑rich adenoma.

t.a: 24‑hour urinary metanephrines or plasma free metanephrines
t.b: Is catecholamine excess present? → Elevated levels confirm pheochromocytoma; if unavailable, use bedside orthostatic BP changes and symptom pattern.
Is cortisol suppressed? → Lack of suppression indicates cortisol‑producing tumour.
Is the ratio >20 with suppressed renin? → Suggests primary aldosteronism; confirm with saline infusion test if possible.
Does cytology show non‑adrenal primary? → Guides systemic therapy; avoid in suspected pheochromocytoma.

b: Hypertensive crisis during manipulation of pheochromocytoma.
Severe hypokalaemia with arrhythmia in primary aldosteronism.
Infection, wound dehiscence after adrenalectomy in HIV/TB patients.
Rapid tumour growth or new metastases indicating carcinoma.
sections.p: Identify life‑threatening hormone excess or malignant spread early.

b: Pheochromocytoma: α‑blockade (phenoxybenzamine or oral doxazosin) → stabilise BP before surgery; avoid β‑blockers alone.
Cortisol excess: ketoconazole or metyrapone to control cortisol if surgery delayed; avoid drugs causing hepatotoxicity in hepatitis B.
Aldosterone excess: spironolactone or eplerenone to correct hypokalaemia and BP; monitor potassium.
Benign non‑functioning adenoma <4 cm: observe with repeat imaging at 6–12 months.
Surgery: laparoscopic transperitoneal adrenalectomy for lesions ≤6 cm; open adrenalectomy for suspected carcinoma or invasive tumour.
If CT/MRI unavailable: rely on ultrasound size and clinical hormone profile; refer for imaging when possible.
sections.p: Treat hormonal excess first, then definitive surgery; adapt to resource limits.

b: Imaging at 6 months, then annually for ≥5 years after carcinoma resection.
Annual blood pressure, electrolytes, and cortisol/aldosterone screening for functional tumours.
Educate patients on avoiding excess stressors that may precipitate catecholamine spikes.
Vaccinate HIV/TB patients and optimise nutrition to reduce surgical complications.
sections.p: Long‑term surveillance prevents recurrence and monitors hormone control.

b: Renal cell carcinoma – originates from kidney, may invade adrenal.
Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumour – can secrete hormones but located posterior to pancreas.
Cushing’s disease – pituitary ACTH adenoma, not adrenal origin.
sections.p: Distinguish adrenal tumours from other abdominal masses and endocrine disorders.

b: Small pheochromocytomas may have normal plasma metanephrines; repeat testing if suspicion high.
Adenomas <10 HU on CT can still be functional; always correlate with hormonal assays.
Renin may be low in severe volume depletion, falsely raising aldosterone‑renin ratio.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden severe hypertension (>180/120 mmHg) with headache or chest pain
Rapidly enlarging abdominal mass or new onset abdominal pain
